etymology: Old English þrescold, the place of treading at a doorway; from þrescan (to thresh), the door-stone where grain was once beaten before entering the house.
biblical_def: The threshold is the stone or beam at the bottom of a doorway — the boundary between outside and inside, sacred and profane, household and street. Scripture treats the threshold as a place to be guarded, honored, and crossed deliberately.
webster_summary: The plank, stone, or piece of timber which lies under a door; the entrance.
webster_full: THRESHOLD, n. The plank, stone, or piece of timber which lies under a door; the entrance to a house or room.
Hence figuratively: the place of beginning, the entering on any business; that which one must cross with intention.
scriptures: Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon's house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day.
Then the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub, and stood over the threshold of the house.
In the same day also will I punish all those that leap on the threshold.
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him.
corruption_summary: The threshold has been flattened into a friction-free doorway; nothing is guarded, nothing is honored, no one is welcomed across.
corruption_paragraphs: Ancient households knew the threshold as a charged place. Friend or stranger, every visitor stopped there; the host crossed first, the guest waited, and a word of welcome carried them in. The threshold was where you decided who belonged inside.

Modern doors slide open automatically. Houses have no real threshold — just a strip of weather-stripping — and households no longer notice who crosses. The result: a home without edges, where strangers are kept out by locks rather than welcomed in by hosts.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the threshold and the doorway as a single ritual zone — the place where the household meets the world.
roots_lines: H4670 — מִפְתָן (miftan) — threshold, doorsill (1 Samuel 5:5; Ezekiel 9:3).
H6607 — פֶתַח (pethach) — doorway, opening, entrance — the wider sense of the threshold zone.
usage: Every threshold is a question: who do you let in?
Bless the door, and you will start to bless the household.
A house without a guarded threshold is a hotel.

etymology: From Latin tabula (board, plank) — the flat surface around which a household ate — plus Old English fēolagscipe (partnership). The shared meal as covenant.
biblical_def: Table fellowship is the act of eating with another as an expression of covenant, hospitality, and shared life. In Scripture, who you eat with names who you belong to; Jesus broke every social wall by sitting down to table with the wrong people.
webster_summary: (Composite term.) The communion of a meal taken together; the fellowship that comes of sharing food.
webster_full: Webster 1828 treats fellowship as “companionship; society; consort; mutual association of persons on equal and friendly terms,” and table as the place at which food is taken.
Joined, the phrase names a particular kind of fellowship: the bond formed by sharing a meal under one roof. To break bread with a man was, in Scripture and in common life, to declare him friend.
scriptures: Also they saw God, and did eat and drink.
And it came to pass, that, as Jesus sat at meat in his house, many publicans and sinners sat also together with Jesus and his disciples.
That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.
And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The shared meal has been replaced by the personal-feed meal: same room, separate plates, separate screens, no fellowship.
corruption_paragraphs: For most of human history, the daily meal was the household's daily covenant renewal: same table, same bread, same blessing, same faces. To miss the meal was to miss the family that day. To bring a guest to the table was to extend the household.

Now meals are eaten in shifts, in cars, in front of separate screens. The table has been replaced by the counter and the couch. The result is not just lonely eating — it is lonely belonging. Households share addresses but not tables, and so they share less and less of anything else.
roots_summary: Both Hebrew and Greek lift the table itself into the vocabulary of communion with God.
roots_lines: H7979 — שֻֻׁוּלְחָן (shulchan) — the table, especially the showbread table in the tabernacle.
G2625 — κατακλίνω (kataklino) — to recline at table; the posture of full, unhurried fellowship.
usage: Table fellowship is slower than the world wants it; that's the point.
Who you eat with, you become like.
If your household no longer shares a table, it has stopped being a household.

etymology: Old English hus-hold (the holding of a house) plus Latin altare (high place of sacrifice). The home's appointed place of worship.
biblical_def: A household altar is the family's appointed station for daily worship — the place where prayer is offered, Scripture read, and God remembered as the one true Lord of this house. The patriarchs built literal stone altars; the New Covenant household keeps the same fire by daily corporate worship under one roof.
webster_summary: (Composite.) An altar erected within or near a private dwelling, for the religious worship of a family.
webster_full: Webster defines altar as “a mount; an elevation; a place on which sacrifices were anciently offered.” A household altar is therefore the family's elevated place — whether literal or appointed by habit — where worship is offered.

In English Christian usage, the term often names the daily family devotional: father, mother, and children gathered for Scripture, prayer, and song. The altar is more verb than noun — it is what the family does, daily, before God.
scriptures: And there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.
He pitched his tent... and there he builded an altar unto the LORD, and called upon the name of the LORD.
But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.
corruption_summary: The household altar was replaced first by the radio, then by the television, then by twelve separate screens; the home no longer bows to anything together.
corruption_paragraphs: Abraham built an altar wherever he pitched his tent. The point was not the stones; the point was that no household of God's people was ever to be without a daily appointment with God. From Abraham to the Puritans, the family altar was assumed.

It is no longer assumed. In most professing-Christian homes, there is no fixed time, no fixed place, no fixed pattern of family worship. The altar has been demolished by accident, replaced by busyness and screens. To rebuild it is the single most repeatable act of household reformation.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the altar by its function: the place of slaughter and offering, the appointed meeting-spot between household and God.
roots_lines: H4196 — מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach) — altar, place of sacrifice; from zabach, to slaughter for offering.
Patriarchal pattern: every new dwelling required a new altar. The tent without an altar was not yet a home.
usage: Rebuild the household altar before you redecorate the house.
If the altar is cold, the marriage will go cold next.
A Marine builds his altar before he builds his career.

etymology: From Old French brasier, a pan of burning coals; ultimately from brese, hot embers. A portable hearth.
biblical_def: A brazier is a metal pan or open vessel for holding burning coals — the portable hearth of the ancient world. Scripture uses it both as the king's winter heater and as a stand-in for any open fire of household or shame.
webster_summary: An artificer that works in brass; or, a pan for holding coals.
webster_full: BRAZIER, n. One whose occupation is to manufacture brass utensils; or by metonymy, a pan to hold coals.
In its second sense, the brazier is the warming-pan around which the household drew in cold weather, and over which guests warmed their hands; a humble, mobile cousin of the fixed hearth.
scriptures: Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.
He cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed.
And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself.
As soon then as they were come to land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.
corruption_summary: The brazier was replaced by the thermostat: heat without gathering, warmth without faces.
corruption_paragraphs: The brazier in Jeremiah 36 was where King Jehoiakim sat to be warm in winter; it was also where, foolishly, he burned the prophet's scroll. Peter denied Christ at one such fire (John 18:18), and was restored by Christ at another (John 21:9). The coal-pan is a quiet character in some of Scripture's sharpest scenes.

Modern central heating is a marvel, but it is not a brazier. Heat without gathering shapes a household differently than heat that requires a circle of bodies. The thermostat warms the room; the brazier warms a fellowship.
roots_summary: The Hebrew word in Jeremiah's palace scene is the same word elsewhere translated hearth.
roots_lines: H254 — אָח (ach) — fire-pot, brazier; the king's winter coal-pan in Jeremiah 36:22.
Note: ancient braziers were the “portable hearth” of life lived in tents and open courts — one fire that traveled with the family.
usage: A brazier in the courtyard is more sociable than a furnace in the basement.
Peter learned twice at a brazier: first to deny, then to be restored.
Where there is a fire, men gather; where there is no fire, men scatter.

etymology: Latin incensum (that which is set on fire) plus altare (high place of offering). The fragrant altar.
biblical_def: The incense altar was the small gold-overlaid altar that stood in the Holy Place, just before the veil of the Most Holy. On it the priest burned a specially compounded incense morning and evening — a fragrant, continual symbol of the people's prayers ascending to God.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The altar of incense; the smaller altar before the veil, on which sweet spices were burned.
webster_full: Webster: incense — “perfume exhaled by fire; the odors of spices and gums, burnt in religious rites, or as an offering to some deity.”

The incense altar of the tabernacle and temple was distinct from the larger bronze altar of burnt offering: it stood inside the Holy Place, was overlaid with gold, and received only the daily incense and the blood of the sin-offering on the Day of Atonement.
scriptures: And thou shalt make an altar to burn incense upon: of shittim wood shalt thou make it.
And Aaron shall burn thereon sweet incense every morning... And when Aaron lighteth the lamps at even, he shall burn incense upon it, a perpetual incense before the LORD.
Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints.
corruption_summary: Prayer has been demoted to private wishful thinking; the picture of prayer as fragrant smoke before God's throne is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is consistent: prayer is incense (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3-4). It is offered, it ascends, it pleases God by its fragrance, and it has weight in heaven. The incense altar made this picture daily and visible to Israel for a thousand years.

Modern prayer is often imagined as a private brain activity that may or may not be heard. The incense altar corrects that: prayer is liturgical, fragrant, and continual. It is not merely sent — it is offered, on an altar, by a priest, before a God who delights in the smell.
roots_summary: Hebrew names both the small altar and the substance burned upon it.
roots_lines: H4289 — מַחְתָּה (machtah) — censer, fire-pan; the implement that carried coals from the burnt-offering altar to the incense altar.
H7004 — קְּטֹרֶת (qetoreth) — the compounded incense itself; sweet smoke offered before the LORD.
usage: Prayer is incense; treat it like an offering, not a tweet.
The morning prayer and the evening prayer are the household's incense altar.
If the smoke does not rise daily, the household is not yet a temple.

etymology: Latin perpetuus (continuous, unbroken) plus Old English fýr (fire). The fire that is never let out.
biblical_def: The perpetual fire was the altar fire God commanded never to go out (Leviticus 6:13). It is the type of every fire God lights and tells His people to tend: the household altar, the watchman's post, the inner devotion of the saint.
webster_summary: Continual fire; a fire kept always burning, especially the altar fire of Israel.
webster_full: Perpetual in Webster: “never ceasing; continual; uninterrupted.”

Applied to fire, it names the altar flame Israel was forbidden to allow to go cold. The priest was charged with feeding it morning and evening, every day of his lifetime — the visible promise that God's presence would not depart while His people kept their watch.
scriptures: It is the burnt offering, because of the burning upon the altar all night unto the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be burning in it.
The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out.
Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee.
corruption_summary: Modern devotion is intermittent — lit on Sundays, allowed to die during the week. The altar fire concept has been quietly forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole point of Leviticus 6:13 is that there is a class of fire God Himself starts and forbids you to let go out. The altar fire is one. The Spirit's indwelling is another (1 Thess 5:19). The prophetic gift is a third (2 Tim 1:6).

We have privatized devotion to the point that “quenching the Spirit” sounds quaint, and a household whose worship has died sounds normal. Recover the perpetual-fire idea and the rhythm of life changes: there are some flames you simply do not let die, even if it costs you sleep, money, or convenience.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a single word for what is constant, daily, unbroken — the same word for the perpetual fire and the perpetual sacrifice.
roots_lines: H8548 — תָּמִיד (tamid) — continually, perpetually; the daily-and-nightly cadence of the altar.
H784 — אֵשׁ (esh) — fire; the substance commanded to be tamid — never out.
usage: There are some fires God lights and forbids you to let die.
Every household has a perpetual fire; the question is whether you tend it.
Quench not the Spirit — that is the New Covenant version of Leviticus 6:13.

etymology: Old Norse kynda (to set on fire); the small dry wood used to start a larger fire. By figure: that which begins zeal.
biblical_def: Kindling is the small, dry, deliberately gathered fuel that gets a fire going. Spiritually, it names the small daily acts — an opened Bible, a knee bent, a song hummed — that the Spirit uses to set a heart and a household ablaze.
webster_summary: Materials for starting a fire; the act of setting on fire.
webster_full: KINDLING, n. The act of setting fire; also, the materials used to begin a fire — commonly small dry sticks or shavings.
Figuratively: any small thing capable of starting a greater zeal, whether of faith, indignation, or love.
scriptures: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue.
But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that compass yourselves about with sparks: walk in the light of your fire.
corruption_summary: We wait for inspiration to fall on us; the saints learned to gather kindling and strike the match.
corruption_paragraphs: Kindling is what you have to fetch before you ever feel warm. The saint who waits to feel inspired before opening Scripture will rarely catch fire; the saint who opens Scripture daily as kindling will, in time, find the heart begin to burn (Luke 24:32).

Modern devotion treats spiritual feeling as weather — arriving uncalled, leaving uncalled. The biblical pattern treats it as fire — lit by deliberate kindling, fed by perpetual fuel, fanned into flame (2 Tim 1:6) by purposeful breath.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek both name the deliberate act of starting a fire; the kindling is what carries the spark.
roots_lines: H1197 — בָּעַר (ba'ar) — to burn, to kindle, to consume.
G381 — ἀναπτω (anaptō) — to kindle, to light up; used by James of the tongue setting forests aflame.
usage: Open the Bible before you feel like it; that's the kindling.
A psalm sung in the kitchen is more kindling than a podcast in the headphones.
If your devotion has gone cold, gather kindling; do not wait for lightning.

etymology: Old English æmerge, the live coal hidden under ash; the still-glowing remnant of a great fire.
biblical_def: An ember is a single live coal still glowing under the ashes — small, easily missed, and sufficient to rekindle a whole fire. Scripture honors the ember: the smoking flax God refuses to quench, the faint faith He fans into flame.
webster_summary: A live coal, covered with ashes; the still-glowing remnant of a fire.
webster_full: EMBER, n. A live coal; the unextinguished remnant of a fire, especially when smothered in ashes.
By figure: any small remaining warmth or zeal, capable of being revived. The saints used ember for the faint surviving spark of faith in a discouraged believer.
scriptures: A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench.
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
And after the fire a still small voice.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.
corruption_summary: Modern Christian discourse trades in firework moments; God specializes in tending embers.
corruption_paragraphs: “Smoking flax” in Isaiah 42:3 is the wick of an oil lamp that has gone almost out — smoke without flame. God's declared posture toward such a flicker is not to snuff it but to nurse it back. He is patient with embers.

We are not. We mistake noise for fire and write off any believer or congregation whose visible flame has dimmed. The ember doctrine corrects us: where God still keeps a coal alive, His people should kneel down and blow.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a specific word for the live coal under ash, and another for the smoldering wick.
roots_lines: H1513 — גֶּחֶל (gechel) — live coal, ember; the seraph touched Isaiah's lips with one (Isaiah 6:6).
H6594 — פִּשְׁתָּה (pishtah) — smoldering flax, the dim wick God refuses to quench (Isaiah 42:3).
usage: Do not despise the smoking flax in your own soul; God doesn't.
Where the ember still glows, kneel down and blow.
A faint coal under ash is enough to start the morning fire.

etymology: Old French lampe (from Greek lampas, torch) plus Old English lēoht. The household's nightly light before electricity.
biblical_def: Lamplight is the soft, oil-fed glow that filled an Israelite home after dark. Scripture uses lamplight to picture the household's steady witness, the Word that lights the path, and the bridegroom's arrival in the night.
webster_summary: The light shed by a lamp, especially as illuminating a room or street at night.
webster_full: LAMPLIGHT, n. The light afforded by lamps; chiefly used to denote nightly indoor illumination, before the advent of gas or electric light.
By extension: any soft, steady, contained light — as opposed to the harsh light of day or the unsteady light of a campfire.
scriptures: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place.
corruption_summary: We have replaced the steady oil-lamp glow with screen-light: brighter, harsher, ever-on, and entirely indifferent to the soul.
corruption_paragraphs: An oil lamp asks for tending. It needs oil; it needs a trimmed wick; it gives a soft light that invites you to slow down. Scripture's metaphors of light are almost all lamplight metaphors — not floodlight metaphors.

Modern indoor light is constant, free, and overwhelming. We never know real darkness, and so the verses about light losing their force. To recover lamplight as a household practice — one candle at supper, lights low for the evening prayer — is to recover a quieter rhythm in which Scripture's light-metaphors actually mean something again.
roots_summary: Hebrew names both the lamp and its standard form — the seven-branched menorah of the sanctuary.
roots_lines: H5216 — נֵר (ner) — lamp; used both of the household oil-lamp and of God's preserving covenant lamp for David.
H4501 — מְנוֹרָה (menorah) — lampstand; in the tabernacle the lamps were always plural, fed continually.
usage: Lamplight asks you to slow down; floodlight asks for nothing.
Read Scripture by lamplight once, and the ‘light unto my path’ verse will mean something new.
Trim the wick before you complain about the dark.

etymology: Hebrew mənôrâh, from nər (lamp); the seven-branched lampstand of the tabernacle.
biblical_def: The menorah is the seven-branched gold lampstand commanded for the tabernacle and continued in the temple. It stood in the Holy Place opposite the table of showbread and was kept burning continually by the priests — a living picture of God's undying light among His people.
webster_summary: The seven-branched golden candlestick of the tabernacle and Jewish temple.
webster_full: MENORAH (Heb. lampstand). The seven-branched candlestick described in Exodus 25, made of one beaten piece of pure gold, with seven oil-lamps mounted upon it.
It is the original referent behind the Greek lychnia rendered ‘candlestick’ in the New Testament; in Revelation 1, the risen Christ walks among seven such lampstands — the seven churches.
scriptures: And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work shall the candlestick be made.
And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always.
I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon.
The seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
corruption_summary: Christians often misread the menorah as a Jewish-only artifact and miss its New Testament reuse: every faithful church is a menorah.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 1 makes the connection unmistakable: the lampstands are the churches, and the risen Christ walks among them, trimming wicks. The menorah is not behind us; it is what every gathered congregation is supposed to be.

Lose the menorah image and you lose the picture of the Church as a continually burning, oil-fed witness in the dark of the world. Recover it, and you remember why the apostle says: be careful how you walk — the lampstand can be removed.
roots_summary: The Hebrew word is a noun built from ner (lamp) with the prefix that means ‘place of’ — literally the place of the lamps.
roots_lines: H4501 — מְנוֹרָה (menorah) — lampstand, candlestick.
H5216 — נֵר (ner) — the individual lamp; seven of these sat on the menorah.
usage: Every healthy church is a menorah — oil-fed, beaten gold, light in the Holy Place.
Christ walks among the lampstands; that is how He pastors His church.
The Spirit is the oil; the menorah is the Body.

etymology: Old French lintel, from late Latin limitellus (small boundary); the horizontal beam over a door, holding back the weight of the wall.
biblical_def: The lintel is the horizontal beam above a doorway. In Scripture it is most famously where Israel was commanded to brush the blood of the Passover lamb — turning every household's doorway into a sign of mercy in the night of judgment.
webster_summary: The horizontal piece of timber or stone over a door, window, or other opening.
webster_full: LINTEL, n. The piece of timber or stone laid horizontally over a door or window to support the weight of the wall above.
Architecturally indispensable, the lintel is also the first surface of the doorway visible from outside — and so, in Israel's Passover, the most public location for the lamb's blood.
scriptures: And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it.
Strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood that is in the basin; and none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning.
When he seeth the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in.
I saw the LORD standing upon the altar: and he said, Smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake.
corruption_summary: The Passover lintel is forgotten as architecture; the doorway has become invisible, and so has the blood that once marked it.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 12 turns every doorway in Goshen into a sermon. The blood on the lintel and doorposts said to the destroyer: this household is covered. The shape of the cross was prefigured in the shape of the door.

Modern households cross their doorways without noticing them. The Passover-lintel image asks: under what blood does my doorway stand? Whose covering does my house claim? The lintel is the household's public testimony — visible from the street — of who has spoken peace over it.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a word for the lintel proper, distinct from the doorposts and the threshold.
roots_lines: H4947 — מַשְׁקוֹף (mashqoph) — lintel, the upper door-beam (Exodus 12:7,22-23).
Note: lintel + two doorposts + threshold form a complete ‘framed doorway’; Passover applied blood to three of the four — the threshold remained clean for crossing.
usage: The blood was on the lintel because the household's testimony belongs out where strangers can see it.
Bless the lintel of your house; the destroyer still walks at night.
The shape of the doorway is the shape of the cross.

etymology: Old English duru (door) plus post (Latin postis, upright timber). The vertical timber that frames an entrance.
biblical_def: The doorpost is the vertical beam on either side of a doorway. Scripture gives it three loaded uses: the place of the Passover blood, the spot where a willing bondservant's ear was pierced, and the surface on which Israel was commanded to write the words of God.
webster_summary: The post or piece of timber on either side of a door, on which the door is hung or against which it shuts.
webster_full: DOORPOST, n. Either of the upright members of the framing of a door.
Scripturally, the doorpost is one of three architectural surfaces (with lintel and threshold) that the Mosaic law charged with covenant meaning.
scriptures: And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses.
Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul.
And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.
And thou shalt write them upon the door posts of thine house, and upon thy gates.
corruption_summary: The doorpost has been emptied of meaning; nothing is written on it, no blood marks it, no covenant ear is pierced beside it.
corruption_paragraphs: Three Mosaic commands meet at the doorpost: cover it (Passover), inscribe it (Shema), and pin a willing servant's ear to it (Exodus 21:6) — signs of redemption, instruction, and gladly chosen service.

Strip the doorpost of those, and you have a board — functional, forgotten. Restore even one of them in symbolic form — a Scripture verse over the doorway, a deliberate moment of crossing — and the household begins to feel like a household under God again.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the doorpost as a structure intended to hold writing — the same word gave rise to the modern mezuzah.
roots_lines: H4201 — מְזוּזָה (mezuzah) — doorpost; the surface God commanded should bear the words of the Shema.
Note: this same Hebrew word now names the small case of Scripture affixed to Jewish doorways — a literal obedience to Deuteronomy 6:9.
usage: Write a verse on your doorpost; the Lord asked for it.
The bondservant who loved his master had his ear pinned to the doorpost — that is the posture of joyful service.
A doorpost without a word on it is a board, not a covenant marker.

etymology: Hebrew məzūzâh, doorpost; by extension, the small case affixed to a doorpost containing the words of Deuteronomy 6:4-9.
biblical_def: Mezuzah is the Hebrew word for doorpost (Exodus 12:7; Deuteronomy 6:9). In Jewish practice it is also the small parchment-and-case fastened to the right side of every doorway, bearing the Shema. Christians have generally let the word fall away — but the underlying command, that the Word of God should be visibly attached to our houses, remains.
webster_summary: (Hebrew, doorpost.) A small case containing a parchment of Scripture affixed to the doorpost of a Jewish house.
webster_full: Webster 1828 does not yet enter mezuzah; it was not common in 19th-century English usage. Modern dictionaries define it as the small case fixed to the doorpost in fulfillment of Deuteronomy 6:9.
Inside the case is a parchment bearing the Shema (Deut 6:4-9) and the second paragraph (Deut 11:13-21), inscribed by hand. The case carries the divine name Shaddai on the outside.
scriptures: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.
And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.
Therefore shall ye lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them for a sign upon your hand.
And thou shalt write them upon the door posts of thine house.
corruption_summary: Christians inherited the command and lost the practice; nothing on most Christian doorposts says the LORD is one.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 6:9 is not abrogated by the New Testament; nothing in the New Testament cancels it. Yet in modern Christian homes there is, typically, no sign at all that this household belongs to the LORD.

A Christian mezuzah-equivalent is a small, deliberate piece of Scripture at the threshold — framed verse, inscribed lintel, even a tiny case — visibly declaring whose house this is. The point is not Jewish observance; the point is Deuteronomy.
roots_summary: The same Hebrew word names both the architectural doorpost and the parchment case attached to it.
roots_lines: H4201 — מְזוּזָה (mezuzah) — doorpost; later, by metonymy, the Scripture-case affixed to it.
Note: traditional mezuzah parchments are inscribed by a sofer (scribe) on the same materials and with the same care as a Torah scroll.
usage: Christians do not need a Jewish mezuzah; they need to obey Deuteronomy 6:9.
Put the Word at the door, and the door starts to mean something.
Whose house is this? — that question should be answerable from the doorpost.

etymology: Latin cohors (enclosure, retinue) plus Old English geard (yard, enclosed space). The household's open inner space.
biblical_def: The courtyard is the open, walled inner space of an ancient house or sanctuary — not the street, not the inner room, but the place where household and guests met under sky. The temple had courts; the household had courts; both were where people actually gathered.
webster_summary: An open court adjacent or within a building; the enclosed area between or behind buildings.
webster_full: COURTYARD, n. A court or area surrounding or contained in a building; a quadrangle.

In ancient Israelite architecture, the courtyard (Heb. chatser) was the social heart of the home: cooking fire, well, livestock, daily life. The temple's outer courts — the Court of the Gentiles, of the Women, of Israel — bear the same word.
scriptures: My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD.
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise.
And as Peter was beneath in the palace, there cometh one of the maids of the high priest.
But he denied, saying, I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest. And he went out into the porch.
corruption_summary: Suburban houses replaced the inner courtyard with the back deck and the privacy fence; the household lost its semipublic gathering ground.
corruption_paragraphs: An ancient courtyard was inside the house but open to the sky — a third space, neither street nor bedroom. Neighbors could be invited in without being escorted to the most private rooms. Cooking, drying laundry, talking with travelers, child's play — all happened there.

Modern American homes have only public-facing front yards (no longer used) and private back yards (often unused too). The courtyard's third-space function vanished; with it, an enormous amount of casual, neighborhood-building life disappeared.
roots_summary: Hebrew uses the same word for the household courtyard and the courts of God's house.
roots_lines: H2691 — חָצֵר (chatser) — court, courtyard; both household enclosure and temple court.
Note: when the Psalmist longs for ‘the courts of the LORD,’ he is using house-architecture vocabulary — the temple is, in his imagination, a home.
usage: Lose the courtyard, and you lose the casual fellowship of neighbors.
Peter denied Christ in a courtyard — the third space is not always safe.
The temple had courts; God's people were never meant to live in pure private.

etymology: Old English innera (further in) plus rūm (space). The household's most withdrawn space; the place of secret prayer.
biblical_def: The inner room is the household's most withdrawn chamber — a closet, store-room, or innermost bedroom where no one passes through. Jesus commands it as the place of secret prayer: “enter into thy closet, and... shut thy door,” out of sight of every audience but God.
webster_summary: An interior or innermost chamber; a private room, removed from the household's public spaces.
webster_full: Webster: chamber — “an apartment in an upper story, or in a story above the lower floor of a dwelling-house, often used as a lodging room, or for retirement and devotion.”
The KJV's ‘closet’ in Matthew 6:6 translates a Greek word for an inner storeroom — not a small wardrobe, but a household's most secluded room.
scriptures: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret.
Thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.
Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment.
He went in therefore, and shut the door upon them twain, and prayed unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: Modern Christians have home offices and reading nooks but no prayer closets; the secret room of devotion has been zoned out of the floor plan.
corruption_paragraphs: Jesus assumes the disciple has access to a place where no one can see him pray — not even the household. The architecture of the ancient home made this easy; the architecture of the modern home, oddly, often does not.

The remedy is not a building project; it is a designation. A corner, a closet, a chair turned to the wall — named, treated as the inner room, defended at a regular hour. Jesus does not require a chamber; He requires a closed door.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a word for the inmost chamber, and the Greek of Matthew 6 names a specific kind of inner storeroom.
roots_lines: H2315 — חֶדֶר (cheder) — inner chamber; the bridal chamber, the storeroom, the secret place.
Note: the Greek tameion in Matthew 6:6 is the household's inner storeroom — lockable, withdrawn, defensible.
usage: Designate an inner room before you ask why you don't pray.
A closed door is not legalism; it is obedience to Matthew 6:6.
The Father who sees in secret is looking for closed doors, not open feeds.

etymology: Possibly a shortening of Middle English sheltron (a shield-troop) or Old English scildtruma — the protective covering. The covered place.
biblical_def: Shelter is covered protection from storm, sun, or enemy. Scripture treats God Himself as the household's deepest shelter, and the household as a small shelter in His larger one — a place of refuge for the weak, the orphan, the stranger, and the wounded.
webster_summary: That which covers or defends from injury or annoyance; a refuge.
webster_full: SHELTER, n. 1. That which covers or defends from injury or annoyance — as a roof, a wall, or a tree.
2. The state of being covered and protected from danger; protection. 3. He that defends — for the LORD is called the shelter of His people.
scriptures: For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy.
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat.
They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter.
corruption_summary: Shelter has been demoted to housing-as-real-estate; the word has lost its protective and pastoral weight.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's shelter language is overwhelmingly relational: thou hast been a shelter; he that dwelleth; under his shadow. Shelter is not a building — it is a person standing between you and the storm.

Reduce shelter to real estate, and the household forgets that its roof is supposed to be the picture of a deeper covering. The Christian home is meant to be a small parable of Psalm 91 — a place where the wounded come in out of the weather and find a person, not just a sofa.
roots_summary: Hebrew has multiple words for shelter, each emphasizing a different aspect: hiddenness, refuge, covering shadow.
roots_lines: H5643 — סֵתֶר (sether) — covering, hiding place, secret shelter (Psalm 91:1; 32:7).
H4268 — מַחְסֶה (machseh) — refuge, shelter from storm; the LORD as place of safety.
usage: A house keeps out weather; a shelter keeps out the destroyer.
If a stranger cannot find shelter under your roof, your roof is just a roof.
Psalm 91 is not a poem about real estate.

etymology: Latin extraneus (foreign) plus Old English wilcuma (one whose coming is wished). The deliberate welcome of the outsider.
biblical_def: Stranger-welcome is the Christian household's practiced obedience to the command, repeated through both Testaments, to receive the foreigner, the traveler, and the unknown guest as if receiving the Lord Himself. It is hospitality with sharper edges — not just to friends, but to those with no claim on us.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The kind reception and entertainment of strangers; the duty of hospitality to those outside one's own circle.
webster_full: Webster: stranger — “a foreigner; one who comes from another country; one of another family or tribe; one unknown; a guest.”
The Christian tradition gathered up these meanings under the New Testament word philoxenia (love of strangers) — an active virtue, not a passive politeness.
scriptures: But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself.
I was a stranger, and ye took me in.
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
corruption_summary: Hospitality has been outsourced to apps and hotels; the Christian household has forgotten that its door was supposed to be the stranger's first stop.
corruption_paragraphs: The early Church grew, in part, by stranger-welcome: traveling believers found beds in private homes, and traveling unbelievers found tables that named the name of Christ. Hebrews 13:2 assumes this as ordinary.

Modern Christians often outsource the entire ministry to nonprofits and short-term-rental platforms. Recovery is not glamorous: a guest room kept ready, a meal stretched, a bed offered before being asked. The strangers come; the question is whether they find a host.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a particular word for the resident outsider, and the New Testament names the corresponding virtue.
roots_lines: H1616 — גֵּר (ger) — sojourner, resident alien; the foreigner whom Israel was specifically commanded to love.
G5381 — φιλοξενία (philoxenia) — literally love of strangers; the New Testament term for hospitality.
usage: Hospitality to friends is good; stranger-welcome is the test.
Keep the guest room ready; the angels arrive unannounced (Heb 13:2).
If your church is full of insiders only, your church has stopped obeying Leviticus 19:34.

etymology: Old English duru (door) plus cēpa (keeper). The one charged with the door.
biblical_def: A doorkeeper is the appointed gatekeeper of a household, palace, or sanctuary — the one who decides who crosses the threshold. Scripture treats the office with surprising honor: the temple gatekeepers were Levites of standing, and the Psalmist would rather serve at God's door than dwell at home in wickedness.
webster_summary: One that keeps a door, especially of a church, public building, or great house.
webster_full: DOORKEEPER, n. One whose office is to attend a door, to admit such as ought to enter, and to exclude others.
In the Old Testament, doorkeepers of the temple were Korahite Levites, given the dignity of guarding God's house. Their roster, with their numbers, is preserved in 1 Chronicles 9 and 26.
scriptures: I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.

All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office.
But Peter stood at the door without. Then went out that other disciple, which was known unto the high priest, and spake unto her that kept the door, and brought in Peter.
For the Son of man is as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch.
corruption_summary: We have shifted the doorkeeper's office to security cameras and apps; no human stands at the door, no human decides who is welcome.
corruption_paragraphs: A doorkeeper is more than a bouncer. He knows the household, knows the regulars, knows who is in trouble and needs to be received quickly, and knows whose entry would be a mercy or a danger. He is, by nature, pastoral.

Most modern households and many churches have automated the doorkeeper out of existence — key fobs, ring cameras, online check-in. Something is gained in efficiency; much is lost in welcome. The Psalmist did not say I had rather be a security camera in the house of my God.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek both name the doorkeeper as a recognized office, with specific guarding responsibilities.
roots_lines: H7778 — שׁוֹעֵר (sho'er) — gatekeeper, porter; the temple office held by the Korahites.
G2377 — θυρωρός (thurōros) — door-keeper; the household servant charged with the entrance (John 18:16; Mark 13:34).
usage: Better a doorkeeper at God's house than a king in your own.
Every household needs a doorkeeper, even if it's only the father with his eyes open.
When the door has no keeper, the wrong things walk in.

etymology: Old French porche, from Latin porticus (covered colonnade). The covered, public-facing platform at the front of a dwelling.
biblical_def: The front porch is the covered, semi-public space facing the street — not yet inside, no longer outside. Functionally, it is the modern household's vestige of the ancient courtyard: a place where neighbors are seen, greeted, and (sometimes) drawn in. Lose it, and the neighborhood loses an organ.
webster_summary: A roofed entrance to a building; an exterior appendage forming a covered approach.
webster_full: Webster: porch — “a portico; a kind of vestibule supported by columns at the entrance of a temple, hall, church, or other building.”

In American usage the front porch became, in the 19th and early 20th centuries, the household's primary tool for casual neighborhood life: a place to sit, watch, talk, hand a stranger a glass of water.
scriptures: And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.
And he went out into the porch; and the cock crew.
All the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering.
And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch.
corruption_summary: The American front porch was traded first for the back deck and then for the attached garage; the household stopped facing the neighborhood.
corruption_paragraphs: From roughly 1880 to 1950, the American front porch was the default evening room: chairs, conversation, neighbors strolling by. Air conditioning ended the practice almost overnight. The household retreated indoors, then to the back deck, then to private screens.

Solomon's Porch in Acts 3 and John 10 was a public covered colonnade where teaching and disputation happened. Recover the front porch as a habit and a household begins to recover its public witness — not by program, but by being visibly present where its neighbors can see it.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the temple's great porch; Greek does the same for the Solomon's Porch of Acts.
roots_lines: H197 — אוּלָם (ulam) — vestibule, porch; the eastern porch of Solomon's temple.
Note: a porch is the architecture of welcome — it exists for the visitor, not for the household.
usage: A front porch is a household's polite way of saying we are home to our neighbors.
The porch died when the AC turned on; the neighborhood died about ten years later.
Sit on the porch in the evening; the rest of the ministry plan can wait.

etymology: Hebrew lechem panim, “bread of the face” — the loaves perpetually set before the face of God on the table in the Holy Place.
biblical_def: The bread of the presence (KJV: shewbread) was the twelve loaves of fine flour set every Sabbath on the gold-overlaid table in the Holy Place — one for each tribe of Israel — and eaten by the priests at week's end. It was not food for God; it was a sign of God's people continually before His face, and of His provision continually theirs.
webster_summary: The shewbread; twelve loaves of fine flour, set on the table in the Holy Place of the tabernacle and temple, renewed every Sabbath.
webster_full: Shewbread in Webster 1828: “Among the Jews, bread placed on the table in the sanctuary every Sabbath, before the LORD; literally, bread of the presence.”

Twelve loaves of fine flour, with frankincense laid on the rows, kept on the table from Sabbath to Sabbath. When changed, the old loaves were eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place — a priestly meal of God's sustaining presence.
scriptures: And thou shalt set upon the table shewbread before me alway.
And thou shalt take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes thereof: two tenth deals shall be in one cake.
Every sabbath he shall set it in order before the LORD continually, being taken from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant.
How he entered into the house of God, and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful for him to eat.
corruption_summary: The bread of the presence is forgotten as a household pattern: that the family table should mirror God's table — bread set out, in His presence, with His people, week by week.
corruption_paragraphs: The Holy Place had three pieces of furniture: lampstand (light), incense altar (prayer), table (bread). The household altar mirrors all three: light, prayer, bread — the daily and weekly meal in God's presence.

Most Christian homes have not lost the bread, only its meaning. Recover the idea: the family meal is a small bread-of-the-presence, set before His face, eaten in His sight, sustained by His provision. Sunday lunch is liturgy.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the loaves by what they sit before: the face of God.
roots_lines: H3899 — לֶחֶם (lechem) — bread; the staple loaf, also the broader word for food.
H6440 — פָּנִים (panim) — face, presence; the bread literally before the face of God.
usage: The Sunday family table is a small bread-of-the-presence.
Twelve loaves — God did not forget any tribe; do not forget any of your children at the table.
Bread before His face is the household's answer to Exodus 25:30.

etymology: Old Norse gestr (a stranger received as a friend) plus Old English rūm (space). The room kept ready for the one who is not yet inside.
biblical_def: The guest room is the household's deliberately reserved space for the traveler, the visitor, the unexpected need. Scripture gives it a heavy weight: the inn at Bethlehem had no kataluma for Mary, and Jesus held the Last Supper in another household's kataluma. Whether the guest room is open or closed has shaped redemptive history.
webster_summary: A room in a private dwelling, kept for the entertainment of guests; an apartment for visitors.
webster_full: GUEST-ROOM, n. A chamber or apartment appropriated to the entertainment of strangers or visitors.

In Greek, the same word (kataluma) is used for both the inn-room that had no place for Mary (Luke 2:7) and the upper room secured for the Last Supper (Luke 22:11). The kingdom turns on which doors open.
scriptures: She brought forth her firstborn son... and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
The Master saith unto thee, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?
Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?
Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers.
corruption_summary: The Christian guest room has been monetized into Airbnb income or zoned into a home office; the household has stopped keeping a room ready for the one who arrives in need.
corruption_paragraphs: Bethlehem's tragedy was a closed guest room. The Last Supper's glory was an open one. Scripture is asking which side of that comparison the Christian household stands on.

Recovery does not require an extra bedroom. It requires reservation: a couch, a corner, a hide-a-bed, kept ready — physically and mentally — for the traveler, the runaway, the friend in trouble. The guest-room habit shapes the household more than the household shapes the guest.
roots_summary: The Greek kataluma — the same word in Luke's nativity and in the Last Supper — sits at the center of the New Testament's guest-room theology.
roots_lines: G2646 — κατάλυμα (kataluma) — lodging place, guest-chamber, upper room; literally a place to loose down a load.
Note: kataluma is not the public inn (pandocheion); it is the household's private guest space.
usage: Bethlehem had no kataluma; the Last Supper found one. Whose pattern is your house on?
Keep the guest room ready; you don't know who's coming.
A monetized guest room cannot be a hospitable guest room.

etymology: Old English gaderian (to bring together) plus plaece (place). The appointed spot for the assembly.
biblical_def: A gathering place is the appointed location where God's people convene — tabernacle, temple, synagogue, house-church, sanctuary. Scripture holds an unbroken line: the LORD does not save isolated individuals only, He gathers a people, and He gives them places.
webster_summary: A place where persons assemble; the spot appointed for an assembly.
webster_full: GATHERING, n. The act of collecting or assembling; an assembly; a meeting.
By extension, a gathering place is the location appointed or recognized for such assembly — whether by command (the tabernacle), by custom (the synagogue), or by hospitality (the household).
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity privatized worship and digitized the assembly; the gathering place was reduced to optional and the assembly to a livestream.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 10:25 is not advice; it is a command, against the manner of some, even in the first century, who had begun to absent themselves. The God of the Bible gathers; His people are called the ekklesia, the called-out assembly.

A streamed service is a mercy for the homebound; it is not a substitute for the gathering. The body needs faces, table, song, and the Lord's Supper — none of which translate fully through a screen. Recover the gathering place — sanctuary, living room, hall — and recover the body.
roots_summary: Hebrew has the appointed-meeting word; Greek has the called-out-assembly word.
roots_lines: H4150 — מוֹעֵד (mo'ed) — appointed meeting, season, place of assembly.
G4864 — συναγωγή (synagōgē) — literally a leading-together; the gathering and its place.
usage: The streamed service is a mercy, not a substitute.
Where two or three are gathered — that is the kingdom's minimum, not the household's maximum.
If your church does not have a gathering place, your church is not yet a church.

etymology: Hebrew ohel mo'ed, the tent of the appointed meeting; the portable sanctuary of Israel before the temple.
biblical_def: The tent of meeting is the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary at the center of Israel's camp during the wilderness years — the appointed place where God came down and met with Moses, with the priests, and with His people. It is the great Old Testament picture of God deigning to dwell in the midst of those who travel.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The tabernacle; the appointed tent in which the LORD met with Moses and with Israel.
webster_full: Webster: tabernacle — “a tent; a temporary habitation; in particular, the tent which Moses erected in the wilderness for the worship of God.”
Three Hebrew phrases describe it: mishkan (dwelling), miqdash (sanctuary), and ohel mo'ed (tent of meeting). The last names its primary purpose: the place of appointed encounter.
scriptures: And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation.
And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend.
Then a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us... and we beheld his glory.
corruption_summary: Christians sometimes treat the tent of meeting as Old Testament background; in fact, John 1:14 says Christ Himself tabernacled among us — the tent of meeting walked into the world.
corruption_paragraphs: John 1:14's eskēnōsen — “he tabernacled” — deliberately echoes the wilderness tent. The whole point: the God who once met His people in a portable tent has now pitched His tent in human flesh, in Jesus.

And the picture continues: the Spirit indwells the believer (1 Cor 6:19), and the saints together are God's temple (1 Cor 3:16). The tent of meeting is not behind us — it is, by the Spirit, around us and in us. Christian gathering is the tent reassembled.
roots_summary: Two Hebrew words form the phrase, and together they make the New Testament's root picture of incarnation.
roots_lines: H168 — אֹהֶל (ohel) — tent, dwelling, tabernacle.
H4150 — מוֹעֵד (mo'ed) — appointed meeting, season; the appointed encounter at the tent.
usage: John 1:14 is the second tent of meeting; this time, in flesh.
Every gathered congregation is the wilderness tent reassembled.
If God came down to meet Moses in a tent, He will meet you in your living room.

etymology: Hearth + side: the place beside the hearth; the literal fireside.
biblical_def: Hearthside is the place beside the hearth — the chair drawn near the fire, the bench by the warming-pan. Scripture does not use the word, but the picture is everywhere: families and travelers gathered close to the household fire to warm hands, share food, and tell what God had done.
webster_summary: The side of a hearth; the place beside the fire; familiar fireside.
webster_full: HEARTHSIDE, n. The side or vicinity of a hearth; the fireside; chiefly used poetically and in domestic prose.
It is the household's informal liturgical space — not the table, not the altar, but the place where stories were told, decisions softened, and the day brought to rest.
scriptures: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house.
Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold... and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself.
As soon then as they were come to land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.
corruption_summary: The hearthside has been replaced by the screen-side; the family no longer sits by the same fire, but stares at separate ones.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 6:7 imagines a parent talking the law of God into a child's heart all day, sitting in the house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. The default mental setting is hearthside conversation — slow, repeated, present.

Modern households talk less. The hearthside has gone screen-side: same room, separate orbits, the fire reduced to background noise on a smart TV. Recover the literal fireside — or even just chairs facing each other — and Deuteronomy 6:7 starts to be possible again.
roots_summary: There is no specific Hebrew or Greek word; the picture rests on hearth-vocabulary plus the verbs of dwelling beside.
roots_lines: H254 — אָח (ach) — fire-pot, hearth; the fire one sits beside.
Note: in the New Testament anthrakia (charcoal fire) frames two of the most loaded fireside scenes — Peter's denial and Peter's restoration.
usage: Pull a chair to the hearthside, and Deuteronomy 6:7 starts to be possible.
Peter learned and re-learned discipleship at a fireside.
The hearthside is the household's informal pulpit.

etymology: Old French oile (from Latin oleum, olive oil) plus Greek lampas (torch). The household's nightly fire-vessel.
biblical_def: An oil lamp is the small clay or metal vessel that held olive oil and a wick — the household's primary light after sundown for most of biblical history. Scripture freights it with weight: the lamp of David, the wise virgins' oil, the lamp of the body, the LORD as the lamp of the new Jerusalem.
webster_summary: A vessel for burning oil with a wick, used to give light.
webster_full: Webster: lamp — “a vessel for containing oil to be burned by means of a wick.”

Israelite household lamps were small open clay dishes or pinched-rim vessels burning olive oil; the wick was twisted flax. They burned for hours but required regular oil and trimmed wicks — the Bible's most pervasive picture of the daily care of the soul.
scriptures: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
And the city had no need of the sun... for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
corruption_summary: Modern light is free; the daily-tending picture of the oil lamp — oil supply, trimmed wick, conserved fuel — has been lost from Christian imagination.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 25 only works if oil is finite and lamps go out. The wise virgins did not feel more spiritual than the foolish; they had simply tended their lamps. Their oil was bought ahead of time.

We live with constant ambient light and forget. Recover the picture — lamp, wick, oil, trimming — and verses across both Testaments come back to life. The household needs tendable light, not just bright light.
roots_summary: Hebrew names the lamp itself, and the New Testament uses both the small household lamp and the larger torch.
roots_lines: H5216 — נֵר (ner) — lamp; David's preserved ‘lamp’ (1 Kings 11:36) and the household's nightly light.
Note: Greek luchnos is the small household lamp; lampas is the larger torch — both are in Matthew 25, depending on translation.
usage: Buy the oil before the cry goes up at midnight.
Trim the wick before you complain about the dim light.
The household with daily-trimmed lamps will not be caught dark.
